title: Use cases and domain entities
idea: Requirement analysis turns a vague brief into use cases (who does what), entities (the nouns with identity) and rules the design must enforce.
points: Each verb an actor performs becomes a use case and a public method.
Nouns with their own identity, such as `Room` and `Booking`, become entities.
Each rule gets one owner: `Booking` checks its own slot, `ConflictPolicy` checks overlaps.
Ask about edge cases early: zero-length slots, back-to-back meetings, cancellations.

code.title: Entities with their rules
code.caption: Times are hours as numbers, so `9.5` means 9:30. Try a booking that ends before it starts.

walk.text: `Room` knows its capacity, so it answers whether a group fits.
`Booking` owns one rule: it refuses an empty or reversed slot.
Overlap belongs to `ConflictPolicy`, not `Booking`. Half-open slots let back-to-back meetings pass.
Each line checks one rule: capacity, overlap, back-to-back and an invalid slot.

pitfalls: Do not make every noun a class; `Floor` may be a plain field of `Room`.
Treat slots as half-open, or back-to-back meetings will be rejected.
Write each rule down with its owner, so it is not checked in two places.

quiz.why: The first pair only touch at 10, and `10 < 10` is false. The second slot sits fully inside the first, so both comparisons hold.

takeaway: Verbs become use cases, nouns become entities, rules find an owner.
